opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say it's a mix of "faster than I expected" and "harder than I expected," depending on which part you look at.

When we started, the core bet was that a model trained natively on how the physical world works, rather than on text first with perception and action added on afterward, would develop a different kind of understanding. It would learn things like continuity, object permanence, and cause and effect directly from data. On that front, I've been pleasantly surprised. Some of the behaviors we see, like keeping a scene consistent over longer horizons or predicting how things move and interact, emerged earlier than I thought they would. There were moments where we looked at the outputs and said, okay, the model clearly isn't just memorizing appearances. It has picked up some structure.

But I also have to be honest about the gaps. Fine-grained physical reasoning is still fragile. Contact, deformation, and precise interactions between objects all fall short. The model can look convincing at a glance and still be wrong in ways that matter if you want to use it for robotics or any real decision-making. Long-horizon consistency is better, but it's not solved. And evaluation is hard. In language we have fairly mature benchmarks. For physical-world models, we're still figuring out what "good" even means beyond "it looks right."

If I had to give a score against my original expectations, I'd say we're ahead on generality and emergent understanding, and behind on reliability and controllability. And those last two are exactly what you need to turn this from an impressive demo into infrastructure.

So my feeling is cautious excitement. The direction is right; I'm more convinced of that now than when we started. But I underestimated how much engineering, data work, and patience it would take to go from "the model kind of gets physics" to "you can trust the model about physics." That second step is where most of our energy is going now.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's been faster than I expected in some ways, and slower in others.

When we started, I thought the hardest part would be getting the model to produce visually convincing video. That turned out to be the easier part. Within about a year, the samples went from something that looked like a broken flip-book to something you could put in front of a non-expert and they wouldn't immediately flinch. Scaling data and compute really did carry us further on appearance than I'd budgeted for.

What's been slower is the part I actually care about, which is whether the model understands the physical world rather than just rendering pictures of it. Does an object persist when it goes behind another one? If a glass falls off a table, does it fall, does it shatter in a way that makes sense, does the liquid behave like liquid? We can get these right in a lot of cases now, but the failure modes are still revealing. The model will often produce something that looks plausible frame by frame while quietly violating some basic constraint over a longer horizon. That gap between "looks right" and "is right" is where most of our effort goes today.

I'd also say my expectations about what "native" means have shifted. Early on I was thinking of it mostly as a video generation problem with better physics. Now I think of it more as building a model whose internal representation is organized around space, time, and interaction, and where generation is just one way to read that representation out. Once you frame it that way, you start measuring progress differently. Not just by how pretty the output is, but by whether the same model can be queried, controlled, and eventually act in a loop with an environment.

So if you ask me to score it, I'd say we're ahead on the surface and roughly on schedule, maybe a little behind, on the depth. But the depth is the whole point, and I'm fairly optimistic, because the failures we see now are the kind you can actually study. Two years ago the failures were just noise.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate what looks promising from what we’ve actually demonstrated. For a physical-world-native model, the important question is whether it can understand how actions change the world and use that understanding reliably in new situations. A convincing example is encouraging, but it isn’t enough to establish that.

So I’d assess progress against that standard: how well the model generalizes, where it breaks down, and whether those failures help us identify what’s missing. Without that evidence, I’d be cautious about saying we’re ahead of or behind expectations.

sol-6.1.text: I’d separate our ambition from what we’ve actually demonstrated. The ambition is a model that learns from and interacts with the physical world. But to assess progress honestly, we need to ask whether it handles unfamiliar situations, whether its behavior is reliable, and whether improvements carry over across tasks. Without concrete results on those questions, I wouldn’t say we’re ahead of or behind expectations. A convincing demonstration is encouraging; dependable performance in the real world is the more meaningful milestone.
